card.title: Poem 2 — A Red, Red Rose (Robert Burns)

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The poem at a glance "A Red, Red Rose" (1794) by Robert Burns is a Scots lyric — a song, really — in which a speaker tells his beloved how long and how deeply he loves her. It is the NEB syllabus's purest lesson in **simile, hyperbole and refrain**: nearly every line is built on one of the three, and the poem works because the comparisons are enormous and the music is simple.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Similes drive the poem: love compared to a red rose and a sweet melody.
Theme: eternal love — 'till a' the seas gang dry' uses hyperbole for devotion.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: Dialect note: 'bonnie', 'gang', 'wi'' — Scots dialect adds intimacy and folk-song quality; mention it for the style mark.  ·  ## The themes worth an essay **Love as intensity, not logic** — the poem never argues; it declares. **Love versus time** — the true antagonist of the poem is not a rival but duration, and love is shown beating it. **Parting and fidelity** — the fourth stanza's real promise: distance is temporary, devotion is not.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The title, defended "A Red, Red Rose" takes its title from the opening simile — the poem's first and most famous image. The defence a candidate should write: the title announces the poem's method (comparison), its tone (fresh, natural, alive) and its subject (love in full bloom) in three words; the doubled "red" is the poem's music beginning before the poem does.  ·  ## How NEB asks it **"What does the poet compare his love to?" (2 marks)** — a red, red rose (sight) and a sweetly played melody (sound): fresh, beautiful, harmonious. **"Why does the speaker use exaggeration?"** — to make love's depth visible; hyperbole is sincerity at full volume. **"What promise does the speaker make in the last stanza?"** — to return however far he must come, however long it takes.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. What two things does the speaker compare his love to? (2 marks) — a red rose and a sweet melody.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **‘A Red, Red Rose’ — simile bank (classified)** | Simile/metaphor | Compares love to | Quality claimed | |---|---|---| | Red, red rose | June-blossoming flower | Freshness, beauty | | Sweet melody | Tune played in tune | Harmony | | Till seas gang dry | Eternal endurance | Timelessness | | Rocks melt wi’ the sun | Geological permanence | Impossible end |  ·  **Structure of the poem** | Stanza | Job | Key image | |---|---|---| | 1 | Declare love via simile | Rose and melody | | 2 | Extend love beyond nature | Dry seas | | 3 | Swear endurance till doomsday | Melting rocks | | 4 | Farewell and promise | Come again though far |

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## Reading it closely, stanza by stanza **First stanza — the declaration by comparison.** The beloved is "like a red, red rose" — the poem's most famous **simile** — and "like a melody that's sweetly played in tune". Notice the strategy: she is not *described*; she is *compared to the most beautiful things the speaker knows*, a June flower and a piece of perfect music.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Simile** — "my luve is like a red, red rose"; "like a melody that's sweetly played in tune": the beloved rendered as flower and music, beauty seen and beauty heard. - **Hyperbole** — seas going dry, rocks melting, ten thousand miles: love declared in units the planet cannot survive.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: The four similes are the poem — rose (beauty), melody (sweetness), the seas drying (eternity), the flower of June (youth); each simile = one mark in analysis.  ·  Trick 2: Hyperbole question: 'till a' the seas gang dry' and 'rocks melt wi' the sun' are deliberate exaggerations of eternal love — name the device and its effect.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. Why does the speaker use exaggeration? (1 mark) — to express the boundless, eternal nature of his love.
